messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Psychologist
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Transportation (Bicycle): Bicycle, Female Presence: Being alone with women, Crowding/Overstimulation: Crowded spaces
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes, Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions, Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger
  Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

James still cannot tell the story. When he tries, the sequence breaks apart. What remains are snapshots: the green fabric of the sofa cushions, the dim kitchen light, his own hand pressed against the wall, the scrape of gravel under his bicycle tire as he arrived home that afternoon. He was thirty-two then, a young psychologist just starting a private practice, and he had been with a woman—Lena—for nearly a year. The abuse had escalated gradually, and that day it culminated in a physical assault that left him with a fractured rib and a conviction he has never fully shaken: that people, especially women he is alone with, are not what they seem.

James is sixty-eight now, still a practicing psychologist, and he is married to a woman he has loved for thirty-five years. None of that has quieted the internal watchfulness. In his office, when a female client closes the door behind her, he feels a flicker of alertness that he has learned to mask with professional composure. He monitors her posture, the angle of her body, the tone of her voice—not clinically, but protectively, searching for the split-second shift that might signal danger. He has come to believe that his own judgment is unreliable; after all, he once trusted Lena, and that trust was shattered. The world, as he understood it, was destroyed in that apartment, and no amount of cognitive reframing has rebuilt it.

The triggers are specific and insistent. He avoids crowded spaces now—the supermarket at peak hours, the waiting room during the clinic’s busiest slots, the annual psychology conference he used to enjoy. The press of people, the unpredictable movements, the difficulty of seeing every face—all of it makes his chest tighten. He also avoids riding his bicycle, though he once loved it. The afternoon of the assault began with a bike ride; the bicycle is now a symbol of the moment just before everything broke. Even the clothes he wore that day—a dark blue jacket, jeans—he has not worn since. He has a small wardrobe of neutral, loose-fitting garments, nothing that resembles the outfit he was in when Lena’s fist connected with his jaw. He never allows himself to feel or express anger; he believes that anger, once released, would be uncontrollable and destructive, and that it would prove he is as dangerous as his abuser claimed he was. Instead, he works hard to keep his emotions flat, even in sessions, even with his wife.

Night is hardest. He wakes often—two, three, four in the morning—and lies still, listening. He checks the bedroom door, the window lock, the shadow of a coat on the hook. There is no reason for it. He is safe. But the body does not believe the mind’s reassurances. The memory sometimes surfaces without an image: a wave of terror that floods him as he sits at his desk, or in the car, or in the middle of a conversation, and he has no idea why. The fear is the same as it was that day, but it is disconnected from any narrative. He can recall specific photographs of the event—Lena’s face contorted, the crack of the lamp against the wall—but he cannot arrange them into a coherent story. He has never told anyone the full account, because there is no full account; there are only fragments and feelings.

Professionally, he has adapted. He sees clients only in his private office, never in a group setting. He has stopped taking evening appointments because the drive home in the dark compounds his nighttime vigilance. His wife has noticed his reluctance to accompany her to social gatherings, especially those with many women present. He says he is tired. He is tired—exhausted from the constant scanning, the emotional suppression, the nightly checks. His PCL-5 score of 61 reflects a severity he can no longer ignore. He came to therapy—his own therapy, as a patient—because he feared that his inadequacy was leaking into his clinical work. He worries he cannot be present for his clients. He worries he cannot be present for himself. More than anything, he wants to believe that the world can be safe, that not every woman is Lena, that he might one day ride a bicycle again without the image of the green sofa cushion rushing back. But at sixty-eight, he is not sure if that hope is realistic or just another belief waiting to be shattered.
